title: National Interest and Power

cards.h: The two oldest words in IR
cards.b:
Every state says it acts for the national interest. Every theory of IR has a view on power. These are the building blocks of foreign policy analysis, and they appear in almost every answer you write.

The problems are real. What exactly is the national interest? Who decides? Is power just guns, or also money, ideas and attraction? Can power be measured?

UPSC likes both direct and indirect questions: "Explain national interest as a determinant of foreign policy", "Distinguish hard and soft power", "Is soft power enough?" You should know Morgenthau, Nye, Lukes and Strange with their books, and be able to link India's examples such as Kautilya, yoga, the diaspora and the nuclear arsenal.

Treat this lesson as a toolkit: definitions first, thinkers next, then the Indian case.

The national interest is what a state believes it must protect or pursue in its dealings with the world. It is often described in terms of security, prosperity, and values.

  • Charles Beard, The Idea of National Interest (1934), studied how the phrase was used in US history.
  • Hans Morgenthau made it central: "interest defined as power" guides a rational foreign policy.
  • Arnold Wolfers (1952) called "national security" an ambiguous symbol: it means different things to different groups.
  • Joseph Frankel, National Interest (1970), split it into aspirational, operational and explanatory uses.
  • Donald Nuechterlein (1976) offered four interests: defence, economic well-being, favourable world order, promotion of values, each with four intensities: survival, vital, major, peripheral.
  • Stephen Krasner, Defending the National Interest (1978), argued that interest is set by the state's central decision-makers.

Types often listed

Vital (core) and secondary; permanent and variable; general and specific.

• Realists: It is objective: survival and power. A wise leader finds it.
  • Liberals: It comes from the preferences of domestic groups, such as business and voters (Moravcsik, 1997).
  • Constructivists: It is shaped by identity and norms. Martha Finnemore, National Interests in International Society (1996), shows states learn interests from international society.
  • Marxists: It hides class interest. The "national" interest often means the ruling class's interest.
  • Critics say the phrase can be a slogan to justify anything, from conquest to secrecy.
  • Bureaucratic politics (Graham Allison, Essence of Decision, 1971): different agencies see different interests.

In a democracy, the interest is debated in parliament, the media and courts. In a closed system, a small group decides.

Good answers say: the national interest is real but contested. Moral claims (human rights, climate) increasingly enter it.

Power is the ability to get others to do what they would not otherwise do (Robert Dahl, 1957). But thinkers have added layers.

Three faces of power

  1. Decision-making (Dahl): who wins open conflicts.
  2. Agenda-setting (Bachrach and Baratz, 1962): who keeps issues off the table.
  3. Preference-shaping (Steven Lukes, Power: A Radical View, 1974): who shapes what people want.

Four kinds of power in IR

Michael Barnett and Raymond Duvall (2005): compulsory (direct force), institutional (control through rules), structural (positions in the system, like creditor and debtor) and productive (shaping identities through discourse).

Susan Strange

States and Markets (1988): structural power sits in four structures: security, production, finance and knowledge.

Kenneth Waltz used a simple scale: power is the combined capabilities of a state. Mearsheimer separates latent power (wealth, population) from actual power (army).

Morgenthau listed nine elements in Politics Among Nations (1948).

Morgenthau's nine

  • Stable: geography, natural resources.
  • Changing: industrial capacity, military preparedness, population.
  • Intangible: national character, national morale, quality of diplomacy, quality of government.

He thought the quality of diplomacy was the most important factor. He called it the "brains" of national power, and national morale its "soul".

Other measures:

  • The Correlates of War Composite Index of National Capability (J. David Singer): iron and steel, energy, military spending, personnel, urban population and total population.
  • China's comprehensive national power approach.
  • Ray Cline's formula (1975) added "strategic purpose and will".

Remember the limits: a large country is not always strong (India, 1962), and a smaller one with will and technology may do well (Israel, Vietnam against the US).

cards.h: Joseph Nye: hard, soft, smart power
cards.b:
Joseph Nye, in Bound to Lead (1990), coined soft power. He developed it in Soft Power: The Means to Success in World Politics (2004).

  • Hard power: the ability to coerce through military force and pay through economic incentives.
  • Soft power: the ability to attract and get others to want what you want. Its sources: culture, political values and foreign policies that others see as legitimate.
  • Smart power: a mix of the two (Nye, The Powers to Lead, 2008; Hillary Clinton used the phrase in 2009).

Sharp power is a newer term (Christopher Walker and Jessica Ludwig, 2017) for authoritarian influence by manipulation and censorship, used for China and Russia.

Nye's later book The Future of Power (2011) argued that power is diffusing from states to non-state actors and from West to East.

Criticisms

Soft power is hard to measure and slow. It works through civil society, not governments. Realists doubt it counts without military backing. It can also backfire if a government's policies contradict its image.

This is Nye's scale, from command (hard) to co-option (soft). Most real policies mix them.

Examples: the Marshall Plan (economic power plus attraction), US-led sanctions (economic coercion), Hollywood and universities (soft), Chinese Belt and Road (economic inducement with soft aims), India's yoga diplomacy (soft).

States turn power into policy through a set of tools. A common list uses the letters DIME: diplomatic, informational, military and economic.

  • Diplomacy: negotiation, treaties, alliances, mediation, summitry.
  • Military: deterrence, compellence, war, arms transfers, training, peacekeeping.
  • Economic statecraft: aid, trade deals, tariffs, sanctions, investment, control of technology and supply chains. In 2025-26 tariffs and export controls became the most visible tools of great powers.
  • Information and culture: broadcasting, education, cyber operations, public diplomacy.
  • Law and institutions: using rules at the UN, WTO and IMF.

Thomas Schelling's distinction is useful. Deterrence aims to stop someone from acting. Compellence aims to make them act or stop acting (Arms and Influence, 1966). Compellence is harder.

The real art is the mix. Using only force can create resistance. Using only attraction leaves a state open to threats.

Power is not always convertible into results.

  • Power paradox. Strong states lose wars against weaker rivals when the weak have more at stake. Andrew Mack's "Why Big Nations Lose Small Wars" (1975) is a classic study. Examples: Vietnam, Afghanistan.
  • Fungibility. David Baldwin argued power is specific to an issue and context. Military strength does not help on climate or trade rules.
  • Nuclear weapons. They give great destructive power but limited usable power.
  • Interdependence. Keohane and Nye: the less dependent actor holds more power.
  • Legitimacy. Power seen as illegitimate invites resistance (Iraq 2003).
  • Time. Power shifts. Power-transition theory (Organski, 1958) says war risk peaks when a rising power nears the leader. Graham Allison's "Thucydides Trap" (Destined for War, 2017) applies this to the US and China.

For the exam, show that power is relational (over whom?), contextual (on what?), and changing (for how long?).

cards.h: Kautilya, national interest and Indian power
cards.b:
Kautilya treated the state's interest (rajya-hita) as supreme. His saptanga theory lists seven elements of the state: swami (king), amatya (ministers), janapada (territory and people), durga (fort), kosha (treasury), danda (army) and mitra (allies). He also named three powers: utsaha (energy), prabhu (military and treasury) and mantra (counsel and diplomacy).

Modern India. Nehru told the Constituent Assembly in 1947 that the art of conducting foreign policy lies in finding what is most advantageous to the country. Article 51 (a Directive Principle) sets goals of peace and international law.

  • Core interests: territorial integrity, energy and food security, development, strategic autonomy, a safe diaspora.
  • Hard power: a nuclear triad, a large army, and rising defence indigenisation. India is among the top five military spenders.
  • Soft power: the International Day of Yoga (21 June, UN resolution of December 2014), Buddhism, Bollywood, ICCR scholarships, ITEC training, Vaccine Maitri (2021), UPI as a digital public good.
  • Economic power: among the world's five largest economies by nominal GDP.

"Explain the concept of national interest. Is it a useful guide for foreign policy?"
"Distinguish between hard power and soft power. Which is more important for India?"
"Examine Morgenthau's elements of national power."
"How does Kautilya's saptanga theory relate to national power?"

Structure: define the term and cite Morgenthau, Nuechterlein and Finnemore. Present who defines the interest (realists, liberals, constructivists). Move to power: Dahl, Lukes, Strange, Barnett and Duvall. Elements of power (Morgenthau's nine). Nye's hard, soft and smart power. Close with India: Kautilya, yoga, diaspora, nuclear and economic capacity.

Always give one critique and one Indian example.

quiz.q: The Idea of National Interest (1934) was written by:
quiz.w: Charles Beard studied the use of the idea in US history.
His 1952 essay argued that the phrase means different things to different people.

quiz.q: Nuechterlein's four basic national interests include all EXCEPT:
quiz.w: The four are defence, economic well-being, world order and promotion of values.

quiz.q: Steven Lukes's Power: A Radical View (1974) described power's:
Susan Strange's structural power rests on:

quiz.w: Nye introduced it in Bound to Lead (1990).

o: Authoritarian influence using manipulation and censorship

quiz.q: In Kautilya's saptanga theory, 'kosha' is the:
quiz.w: Kosha is the treasury; durga is the fort, danda the army, mitra the ally.

quiz.q: Morgenthau considered which element the most important?
quiz.w: He rated diplomacy as the most important factor, the brains of national power.

quiz.q: Which book argues that agencies see different interests, challenging the 'rational state' view?
quiz.w: Graham Allison's study of the Cuban Missile Crisis.
